questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman presented with fevers and night sweats for the last month with weight loss of 15 pounds during the same period. There was no cough or shortness of breath. She was known to have HIV but was nonadherent to her antiretroviral medications and did not engage regularly in care. Investigations: CD4 count 15 cells/μL Blood cultures negative CXR: unremarkable CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis: diffuse lymphadenopathy above and below the diaphragm; mild splenomegaly Mycobacterial blood cultures negative Bone marrow biopsy: acid-fast bacilli seen on microscopy; mycobacterial cultures at 37 oC negative; subcultures at 30 oC positive
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely organism?
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium genavense Mycobacterium avium complex is the most common cause of disseminated NTM infection in AIDS patients. M. genavense, on the other hand, can present in a similar way in AIDS patients and should be considered when patient presents with classic picture of disseminated MAC infection, but the routine AFB cultures remain negative. Incubation of the culture at lower temperature can assist in the recovery of this organism.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q30

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of worsening nonproductive cough. He had chronic obstructive lung disease managed with home nebulizers. He had tried a course of a quinolone antibiotic, which resulted in little improvement in his symptoms. He had no fever, chills, or sweats. He had a 5 lb weight loss in the past 6 months. On exam, he was afebrile and had few scattered expiratory wheezes. Investigations: CXR: no infiltrates High-resolution chest CT: multi-focal bronchiectasis and multiple small nodules Expectorated sputum grew Mycobacterium avium complex
questions.lead_in: What is the best next step in this patient’s management?

options.text: Hold off treatment until sensitivities are available
Send an additional expectorated sputum sample for AFB-smear and culture
Start therapy with ethambutol, rifampin, and clarithromycin
Start quadruple therapy with ethambutol, rifampin, isoniazid, and pyrazinamide

questions.explanation: Send an additional expectorated sputum sample for AFB-smear and culture The patient has risk factors for infection due to M. avium complex (MAC) but requires additional testing to make the official diagnosis with a sputum sample for AFB smear and culture. The medications contain toxicities, and it would be best to provide further work-up to diagnose MAC lung disease before beginning treatment with multidrug therapy. He does not need a bronchoscopy as he is able to expectorate sputum.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q5

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman was evaluated for a dry cough with moderate exertional dyspnea, which had remained stable in intensity over the past 8 months. She had occasionally been treated with antibiotics as an outpatient without any change in her symptoms. She had no systemic signs or symptoms. She was a nonsmoker and took no medications. On physical examination, vital signs were normal. Pulmonary auscultation revealed scattered rhonchi. The remainder of the examination was normal. Investigations: CT lungs: nodular infiltrates, mostly confined to the right middle and bilateral upper lobes Induced sputum: smear for acid-fast bacilli negative; culture positive at 24 days for Mycobacterium avium complex
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Repeat sputum acid-fast bacilli smear and culture

questions.explanation: Repeat sputum acid-fast bacilli smear and culture The patient requires a repeat acid-fast bacilli smear and culture before treatment is initiated. Nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) are easily recovered from the environment, and when they are isolated from nonsterile sites, results require interpretation within the context of the patient’s clinical syndrome to avoid treating colonization. Along with symptoms and CT findings, this patient requires a second positive MAC culture that can be obtained from sputum sample, bronchial wash or lavage, or a histopathologic specimen so that official diagnosis can be established.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q4

needs: Chapter 310 — Infections in the Immunocompromised Host
questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presented with disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection. He had a past medical history of recurrent nontyphoidal salmonellosis. Investigations: HIV Ag/Ab negative HIV VL not detected
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A defect in the IL-12 or interferon-gamma pathway
A defect in the IL-17 pathway
A defect in the IL-21 pathway

questions.explanation: A defect in the IL-12 or interferon-gamma pathway Inherited defects of innate immunity of the IL-12 or IFNgamma pathways present with disseminated mycobacterial and Salmonella infections. In countries where Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination against tuberculosis is recommended, a common presentation of this disorder is disseminated BCG infection. Defects in the IL-17 pathway lead to chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, while defects in the IL-21 pathway lead to hepatobiliary cryptosporidiosis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q41

questions.question: A 7-year-old girl has Mycobacterium avium complex cervical lymphadenitis.
questions.question_raw: PM Q24. MAC lymphadenitis in 7-year old girl.

parts.text: List treatment options (3).
What is the best option and the associated complication?

parts_raw.text: a) List treatment options (3).
b) What is the best option and the associated complication?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Surgical excision of the involved node (excision preferred over needle biopsy). (2) Macrolide (clarithromycin/azithromycin)-based multidrug regimen (with ethambutol +/- rifampin) reserved for recurrent disease or when surgery is high-risk. (3) Observation, since many immunocompetent children have localized disease that drains and self-resolves over ~1 year.
b) Surgical excision is the treatment of choice. Associated complication: cutaneous fistula/sinus tract formation (most frequent after needle biopsy or incomplete excision); operative injury to the facial nerve is the other classic risk.
questions.beyond_mandell: Facial nerve injury as an excision complication is standard surgical/pediatric ID teaching, not stated explicitly in Mandell.

cohort_answer.text:
Treatment options: Surgical excision (bx before for culture), do x-ray to r/o lung involvement; Azithro/clarithro + EMB +/- Rifampin
Best option: Surgical excision. Complication: recurrence, draining fistula formation, damage to facial nerve

questions.question: A man has a Mycobacterium chimaera infection related to his heart transplant (cardiac surgery).
questions.question_raw: 4. Man has mycobacteria chimera infection due to heart transplant.

parts.text: What device is implicated in this?
The device is in your hospital but cannot be removed. What are two things you could do intra-operatively to reduce transmission of this infection?
This man comes in for investigations. What isolation precautions should he be under?

parts_raw.text: a) What device is implicated in this?
b) The device is in your hospital but cannot be removed. What are two things you could do, intra-operatively, to reduce transmission of this infection?
c) This man comes in for investigations. What isolation precautions should he be under?

questions.model_answer:
a) The contaminated heater-cooler unit used during cardiopulmonary bypass (e.g., Stockert/LivaNova 3T), which aerosolizes M. chimaera from its water circuit.
b) (1) Position/vent the heater-cooler unit away from the operative field and the ultraclean (laminar-flow) air path, directing its exhaust fan away from the surgical site. (2) Reduce aerosolization by sealing the unit, using manufacturer-recommended water/air filters, and following strict water-management and disinfection protocols.
c) Standard precautions only - M. chimaera is not transmitted person-to-person, so no special isolation is required.
questions.beyond_mandell: Heater-cooler-associated M. chimaera outbreaks are not covered in this Mandell chapter; answer based on CDC/FDA and ECDC outbreak guidance.

cohort_answer.text: Device: contaminated heater-cooler devices (Stockert 3T, LivaNova PLC). Intra-op measures: ensure maintenance of laminar flow in OR to not disrupt positive pressure; have air/water filters installed in heater coolers to filter bacteria; reduce aerosolization of water tank via tight sealing and directing fan away from procedure. Isolation: No precautions needed - standard

questions.question: Mycobacterium avium complex pulmonary disease.

parts.text: According to published guidelines, name 3 clinical or radiological findings you need for diagnosis (non-microbiological).
What is the one drug in which susceptibility to it portends an overall improved prognosis of cure?
How many drugs would you use and why?

parts_raw.text: According to published guidelines, name 3 clinical or radiological findings you need for diagnosis (non-microbiological)
What is the one drug in which susceptibility to, portends an overall improved prognosis of cure?
How many drugs would you use and why?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Symptoms compatible with MAC pulmonary disease (e.g. chronic cough, sputum, constitutional symptoms). (2) Chest imaging compatible with MAC - nodular or cavitary opacities on CXR, or CT showing bronchiectasis with multiple small nodules. (3) Appropriate exclusion of other diagnoses that could account for the picture.
b) A macrolide (clarithromycin/azithromycin) - the only drug class with a proven correlation between in vitro susceptibility and clinical outcome.
c) At least three active drugs. A multidrug regimen is essential to prevent emergence of macrolide resistance, which markedly worsens prognosis.

questions.question: Mycobacterium avium complex pulmonary disease.

parts.text: Name 3 clinical and radiographic (NOT microbiologic) criteria in the ATS diagnostic criteria.
Name 1 antibiotic to which, if susceptible, means better prognosis.
The MAC is susceptible to the above antibiotic; how many drugs are required to treat it? What is the rationale for this?

parts_raw.text: Name 3 clinical and radiographic (NOT microbiologic) criteria in the ATS diagnostic criteria
Name 1 antibiotic to which if susceptible, means better prognosis
The MAC is susceptible to above antibiotic, how many drugs are required to treat it? What is the rationale for this?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Symptoms compatible with MAC pulmonary disease. (2) Radiographic abnormalities compatible with MAC (nodular/cavitary opacities on CXR; bronchiectasis with multiple nodules on CT). (3) Reasonable exclusion of other diagnoses.
b) A macrolide (azithromycin or clarithromycin) - the only class with susceptibility that correlates with clinical outcome.
c) Three drugs. Rationale: at least two, and usually three, active agents are needed to prevent emergence of resistance (especially macrolide resistance) and improve cure rates.

cohort_answer.text: ATS criteria: Pulmonary or systemic symptoms (chronic cough, dyspnea, sputum production); Pulmonary nodules, bronchiectasis, cavitations. Better prognosis antibiotic: Azithromycin. Drug regimen: 3 drug regimen to prevent induction of resistance

questions.question: You see a patient with Mycobacterium avium complex pulmonary infection.
questions.question_raw: You see a patient with Mycobacterium avium complex pulmonary infection.

parts.text: List the THREE antibiotics that should be used.
The patient refuses to take three antibiotics but agrees to take two. Which TWO antibiotics should be included? Justify your answer microbiologically.

parts_raw.text: List the THREE antibiotics that should be used.
The patient refuses to take three antibiotics but agrees to take two. Which TWO antibiotics should be included? Justify your answer microbiologically.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) A macrolide - azithromycin (preferred) or clarithromycin. (2) Ethambutol. (3) Rifampin (a rifamycin).
b) Macrolide + ethambutol. Microbiologic justification: ethambutol is more effective than any other class at protecting the macrolide against emergence of resistance, and macrolide-plus-ethambutol is the only two-drug combination sanctioned by ATS/IDSA for MAC lung disease. A fluoroquinolone must never be paired with a macrolide as a two-drug regimen because it does not protect against (and may antagonize) macrolide resistance.

questions.question: Pulmonary Mycobacterium avium complex disease (2022).

parts.text: As per ATS guidelines, 3 criteria (clinical and radiographic) requiring treatment.
Which antibiotic, if susceptible, has good prognosis?
Number of drugs needed to treat and why.

parts_raw.text: As per ATS guidelines, 3 criteria (clinical and radiographic) requiring treatment
Which antibiotic if susceptible has good prognosis
Number of drugs needed to treat and why

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Symptoms compatible with MAC pulmonary disease. (2) Compatible radiographic findings (nodular or cavitary opacities on CXR; bronchiectasis with multiple nodules on CT). (3) Exclusion of other diagnoses. Treatment is particularly favoured in those with cavitary disease given the risk of progression.
b) A macrolide - azithromycin (or clarithromycin) - susceptibility correlates with better culture conversion and outcome.
c) Three drugs (macrolide + ethambutol + rifampin). Rationale: multidrug therapy prevents emergence of macrolide resistance and improves cure; ethambutol and the rifamycin protect the macrolide.

cohort_answer.text:
3 diagnostic criteria (ATS/IDSA NTM Guidelines): 1. Clinical - clinical symptoms (pulmonary or systemic) and alternate diagnoses ruled out. 2. Radiologic - CXR with nodular or cavitary opacities; CT with bronchiectasis and nodules. 3. Microbiologic - expectorated sputum cultures x2 with same organism, or BAL + culture x1, or transbronchial/lung biopsy culture x1 and histologic features (or histologic features and sputum/bronchial wash + culture x1). Offer treatment to those meeting diagnostic criteria, especially with AFB smear positive or cavitary lesions.
Antibiotic with good prognosis: Macrolides, clarithromycin specifically the only one with breakpoints; macrolide-susceptibility associated with better culture conversion in macrolide-containing vs macrolide-free regimens.
Number of drugs and why: 3 drugs. ATS recommends a three-drug regimen including a macrolide. Preferred regimen for nodular-bronchiectatic disease is 'RE-MAC': rifampin, ethambutol, macrolide (azithromycin). Add IV amikacin (or streptomycin) if severe or cavitary disease initially. Treatment duration 'at least' 12 months after culture conversion.

questions.question: You are treating a patient with pulmonary nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) infection.
questions.question_raw: You are treating a patient with pulmonary NTM infection.

parts.text: What is the MOST common NTM in Canada?
What are the two MOST common sites of NTM infection, outside of pulmonary?
What are three fast-growing NTM (genus and species)?
What are three criteria you would use to confirm pulmonary NTM?

parts_raw.text: What is the MOST common NTM in Canada?
What are the two MOST common sites of NTM infection, outside of pulmonary?
What are three fast-growing NTM (genus and species)?
What are three criteria you would use to confirm pulmonary NTM?

questions.model_answer:
a) Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) - the most frequently recognized pathogen; in Canada M. xenopi is the second most frequently isolated NTM after MAC.
b) (1) Lymphatic - cervical lymphadenitis (especially children) (2) Skin and soft tissue.
c) (1) Mycobacterium abscessus (2) Mycobacterium fortuitum (3) Mycobacterium chelonae.
d) ATS/IDSA criteria - all of: (1) Pulmonary symptoms plus nodular/cavitary opacities on CXR, or HRCT showing multifocal bronchiectasis with multiple small nodules; (2) Exclusion of other diagnoses (e.g., tuberculosis); (3) Microbiologic confirmation - two positive sputum cultures, OR one positive bronchial wash/lavage, OR a lung/transbronchial biopsy showing granulomatous inflammation or AFB with one positive respiratory culture.

questions.question: A 14-year-old presents with a submandibular nodule that is purple in colour and non-tender; aspiration shows acid-fast bacilli.
questions.question_raw:
Q71 (2016 AM)
14 year old with submandibular nodule. Purple color, not tender. An aspiration showed acid fast bacilli.

parts.text: Name the species and genus.

parts_raw.text: A) Name the species and genus

questions.model_answer: Mycobacterium avium complex (genus Mycobacterium; species M. avium / M. intracellulare, usually grouped as M. avium-intracellulare) - the most common cause of nontuberculous cervicofacial lymphadenitis in children.

questions.question: A 14-year-old presents with a submandibular nodule that is purple in colour and non-tender; aspiration shows acid-fast bacilli.
questions.question_raw:
Q71 (2016 AM)
14 year old with submandibular nodule. Purple color, not tender. An aspiration showed acid fast bacilli.

parts.text: Optimal management strategy?

parts_raw.text: B) Optimal management strategy?

questions.model_answer: Complete surgical excision of the involved node is the treatment of choice (excision preferred over needle biopsy, which risks fistula formation). When excision is complete, concomitant antibiotics are usually not required. Reserve a macrolide-based multidrug regimen (clarithromycin/azithromycin + ethambutol +/- rifampin) for recurrent disease or when surgery poses high risk; some cases are self-limited and need no intervention.

cohort_answer.text: Excisional bx - 95% success. If recurrent disease or in children with high surgical risk, consider clarithromycin-based multidrug regimen (as used for pulmonary disease): clarithromycin, ethambutol, rifampin

questions.question: A 65-year-old smoker with a significant respiratory history presents with Mycobacterium avium complex isolated from sputum on three occasions.
questions.question_raw: Q18 (2008). 65 year old smoker with +++ history presents with MAC in sputum x3

parts.text: 2 indications to treat MAC.

parts_raw.text: A) 2 Indications to treat MAC

questions.model_answer: (1) Meeting the ATS/IDSA case definition - compatible symptoms plus compatible chest imaging plus microbiologic confirmation (e.g. two positive sputum cultures) - i.e. established pulmonary disease rather than colonization. (2) Fibrocavitary/cavitary or advanced radiographic disease, which warrants treatment (and more intensive therapy) because of the risk of rapid, destructive progression.

cohort_answer.text: Fibrocavitary disease - generally warranted at initial dx due to risk of rapid progression/destructive disease. AIDS patients (localized lymphadenitis or disseminated disease) - prompt treatment warranted with anti-MAC therapy and ART. Nodular bronchiectatic disease - can observe, treat if disease progresses (change from smear-negative to smear-positive, increasing quantitative culture, cavitation, worsening nodularity). Observation reasonable with minimal sx/mild CT findings or significant comorbidities. Low BMI is RF for progressive disease. (speaker notes: needs clinical symptoms AND radiographic evidence of disease; two or more samples growing the same thing)

questions.question: A patient has pulmonary Mycobacterium avium complex infection.

parts.text: Name the 3 medications you would recommend for his treatment regimen, assuming it is susceptible.
Patient refuses to take 3 drugs but is willing to take 2 drugs. Which 2 do you choose, and give a microbiologic reason why.

parts_raw.text: Name the 3 medications you would recommend for his treatment regimen, assuming it is susceptible.
Patient refuses to take 3 drugs, but is willing to take 2 drugs. Which 2 do you choose, and give a microbiologic reason why

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Azithromycin (macrolide of choice). (2) Ethambutol. (3) Rifampin.
b) Azithromycin + ethambutol. Microbiologic reason: ethambutol is the drug most effective at protecting the macrolide against emergence of resistance, and macrolide-plus-ethambutol is the only two-drug regimen accepted by ATS/IDSA for MAC lung disease. A macrolide should never be paired with a fluoroquinolone (or rifamycin) as the sole partner, as this fails to prevent - and may promote - macrolide resistance.

cohort_answer.text: 3 medications: Azithromycin; Rifampin; Ethambutol. 2 drugs if refusing 3: Azithromycin; Ethambutol. Reason: Combination of macrolide and fluoroquinolone/rifamycin have been reported to lead to macrolide resistance
